[2026-09-04, 7.31.26 sweep] Corroborating citation found: 'The Avalon Plantation Marker Story' AHA/Auburn panel transcript (Nov. 10, 2020) refers to this same mother as 'Eliza Jones' (rather than 'Elizabeth') and states she and her three biracial children were manumitted in 1820 upon Lewellen Jones's death; panelists speculate (unproven) that the children's father was either Alexander Jones or Lewellen Jones. Jones and Alexander P. Jones to emancipate certain slaves therein named,' Acts Passed at the Second Session of the General Assembly of Alabama (Cahawba, 1820), approved Dec 11, 1820 (Internet Archive OCR) — a mulatto woman named Elizabeth, aged 40; a mulatto girl named Evelina, aged 13; a mulatto girl named Ann, aged 6; and a mulatto child named Shandy, 3 — on the single condition that the two Joneses post bond to the Madison County court chief justice, approved by the county court, securing that none of the four ever becomes chargeable to Alabama or any county or town therein. Legislative manumission, not self-purchase. The act states no kinship, names no father, gives no gender for Shandy, and gives no surnames. CORRECTION to the pending 'Eliza = Elizabeth' treatment above: do NOT merge — Elizabeth (b. ~1780, 40 in 1820) is not Eliza Jones, mother of Columbus (d. fall 1861 at her son's home); the age math makes the identification remote (Elizabeth would have been ~47 at Columbus's ~1827 birth, ~53 at Reuben's, ~63 at Turner's). Also do NOT merge with Elizabeth wf Jerry McCauley, the deceased Elizabeth Jones (both named in Columbus's 1867 bank account), or Elizabeth, 11, in Shandy's 1860 Tuscaloosa household (his daughter). Post-1820: no record found — absent from Boucher's 1830/1840/1850 Madison free-negro head lists. Parents unresolved; children's father unresolved; prior ownership within Lewellen Jones's estate is a strong lead (scholarship + timing — will recorded Apr 1820, act passed Dec 1820), not proven. SJR25 (2017) gives the emancipation as Dec 1, 1820 — one day off the act's printed Dec 11; flag, don't adopt.

Evidence: Bedford County, Virginia chancery cause 1841-044: Benjamin Moore v. Benjamin Perkins et als, County Court of Bedford in Chancery (bill + subpoena dated 20 November 1820; dismissed at September 1841 rules; firsthand visual read of all PNGs, no OCR; read 2026-09-23). Moore alleged these 14 enslaved people were Benjamin Perkins's property, fraudulently put in the possession of his brother Richard Perkins under formal bills of sale as a means of covering the property from Benjamin Perkins's creditors; Richard Perkins was actually removing them westward under the care/management of Woodson Dowdy. Moore asked the court to decree the 14 to him 'they being the proper slaves of the sd Benjn Perkins & their increase if any of the females of them.' Names as written in the BILL (primary). The anti-removal writ (img-0006) repeats names with partially variant/uncertain readings: 'Rebeky' [vs Delphy?], 'Betsy' [vs Polly?], and a trailing 'Steven' [uncertain]; bill spellings taken as primary. Named in the bill as 'Billy a Waterman' — one of the 14.

Evidence: Daughter of Lane Jones and Anne Barber (Henley family Bible via Cary 1897); married John Jones 1759. CORRECTION: the 1966 chart's 'John Jones, son of Lane' is an error — John was Lane's son-in-law, Frances's husband. Four converging records: 1761 York Co. special verdict (names Frances Barber Jones among Lane's children); 1763 Cumberland Co. deed ('John Jones and Frances Barber Jones, his wife, of Louisa County' among Lane's heirs); 1792 Bedford deed (Capt. John Jones and Frances Barber Jones selling 314 ac); Bedford chancery read pass (John Jones's widow 'Frances B. Jones').
Notes: Mother of Llewellyn Jones — this is the link that fixes the lineage. Do NOT merge with the Frances rows 102, 110, 1271, 1905 (different women).

Evidence: Styled 'Captain' (militia title; Rev War service unverified). Married Frances Barber Jones 1759 — son-in-law of Lane Jones, not son. 'Of Louisa County' 1763; Bedford Co., VA by the 1790s; d. intestate ~1796 leaving 'an estate both real and personal to a large amount.' 1792 deed with Frances sold 314 acres (Bedford Deed Bk T p. 97); 1789 receipt gave son-in-law Philip Burton £180 VA currency plus ten enslaved people as a daughter's marriage portion. Children per Bedford chancery read pass (6 cases, 1805–1841): Llewellyn, Charles D., Elizabeth (m. Jesse Anderson), Nancy T. (m. Nelson Dawson); a possible Burton daughter unresolved.
Notes: Father of Llewellyn Jones. Do NOT merge with any other John Jones row (96, 126, 134, 218, 1105, 1206, 1838, 1953 — all different men).

Evidence: Only son of Orlando Jones and Martha Macon; b. June 15, 1707, St. Peter's Parish, New Kent Co. (parish register via Cary 1897); m. 1727 Anne Barber, daughter of Maj. William Barber. Six children (Henley Bible; 1761 York verdict): Martha, Anne, Lane Jr., Rowland, Frances (Barber Jones, b. Jan 26, 1740), William. Wealth: inherited Tidewater estate; tobacco; the Barber marriage folded a magistrate/Burgess father-in-law and the Archer/Hubard kin network into the line.
Notes: Great-grandfather of Llewellyn Jones. Do NOT merge with the enslaved people bequeathed 'to Lane Jones' in Orlando's 1719 will (DB2 rows 1159–1167) — those are people he enslaved, not him.

Evidence: Son of Rev. Rowland Jones. Planter, tobacco shipper, landlord, Burgess for King William Co. (1714, 1715, 1718). Married Martha Macon Jan 31, 1703 (d. May 4, 1716; one son Lane, one daughter Frances who married Col. John Dandridge), then Mary Elizabeth Williams. Died June 12, 1719 at the Queen's Creek mansion; will proved Yorktown Nov 16, 1719. Wealth: tobacco cargo, plantations, a Williamsburg rental tenement, livestock, ~21 enslaved people; died heavily in debt (Williamsburg house ordered sold). Via tombstone, parish register, Burgess lists, Cary 1897.
Notes: Great-great-grandfather of Llewellyn Jones. Tobacco shipment is documented; ship ownership is not — keep the distinction. The enslaved people he bequeathed (DB2 rows 1158–1176) are separate entries.

Evidence: First rector of Bruton Parish, VA (1674–1688); b. 1644 Swinbrook, Oxfordshire; Merton College, Oxford (matric. Nov 11, 1663); d. Apr 23, 1688, aged 48 (tombstone, Bruton churchyard). Also a substantial planter: will Aug 15, 1687 (proved Dec 13, 1688, Yorktown) left son Robert a 400-ac Pomonkey Neck plantation, son William 200 ac on Chickahominy Swamp, daughter Anna Maria 6,000 lbs tobacco and silver, widow Anne the dwelling and plantation for life then to son Orlando — plus enslaved people. 'By no means dependent upon his ministerial salary' (Cary 1897).
Notes: The immigrant generation; father of Orlando Jones. Do NOT claim ship ownership or transatlantic slave trading for him — the documented mechanism is tobacco plantations worked by enslaved labor. Do not merge with his father Rowland Jones (1608–1685).

Evidence: Vicar of Wendover (1664) and Dorney (1667–1685), Buckinghamshire, England; B.A. Christ Church, Oxford, 1632; rector of Little Kimble 1661. Will dated Sept 1, 1665: a comfortable but modest clerical estate — books and manuscripts and £25 to son Rowland, £5 bequests to the other children. Via Cary 1897.
Notes: Father of Rev. Rowland Jones; the English root of the line. The Welsh-origin tradition in some compiled genealogies is unresolved — Cary documents an Oxfordshire/Buckinghamshire clerical family and says nothing of Wales.

Evidence: Wife of Turner Moore and mother of Columbus Jones per Fred C. Rathbun's extraction of Columbus Jones's Freedman's Bank account 29 (M816 Roll 1, acct. 29, 2 Oct 1867); died fall 1861 at her son's home. Columbus, Turner, and Reuben carried her Jones surname. See DB1 rows 1718–1737 (Rathbun fold).
Notes: HYPOTHESIS ONLY — unproven, do not treat as fact: if Eliza was enslaved by the Jones family while Turner was held by a Moore, the family could have formed across two neighboring plantations — the "abroad marriage" pattern — with the children carrying the mother's Jones surname. The 1860 slave schedule puts Alexander P. Jones (96 enslaved, stamped pp. 483–484) adjacent to Benj. T. Moore (stamped 487–488) in the NW Division. Forced separation by sale is unsupported; the mechanism is unknown. Do not merge Eliza with any enslaver's holding without direct evidence. Enslaved son of Edmund Townsend; $10,000 bequest in 1833 will (broken by heirs). Source: Madison County Heritage Book (1998), 'The Jones Homeplace,' p. 78. Edmund Townsend (b. 1791, Lunenburg Co., VA) held ~300 enslaved people on 6,000 acres in Madison County ($88,000 appraisal at his death April 12, 1833). His January 25, 1833 will attempted to free and provide for his enslaved children; white relatives broke the will and the court ordered all property sold 'including the children.' See DB1 row 2689. Do not merge with other same-name individuals without evidence.

Evidence: Named in Bedford County Deed Book 11, p. 22: bill of sale dated Jan. 10, 1794, Charles Gwathin of Bedford to Matthew Merchant (recorded as 'Merchant Matt,' merchant of Bedford), 'one negro woman named Sally.' Named again Deed Book 11, p. 27: Matthew Merchant emancipated 'a certain Negro Woman named Sally,' identified as the woman purchased from Charles Gwathins under the bill of sale now of record, Feb. 25, 1799 — 'forever quit Claim Set free & liberate the said Sally together with all her future increase.' Signed by Matthew Merchant (his mark); acknowledged Feb. 25, 1799.
Notes: Sale-to-emancipation sequence spans five years (1794-1799). Seller Charles Gwathin is the same man who stood surety on Sheriff Thomas Logwood's bonds (Deed Book 11, pp. 10-11). Buyer 'Merchant Matt' (p. 22) is identified as Matthew Merchant by the p. 27 emancipation. Preserve 'Gwathin/Gwathins' spelling variants; do not merge with Gwathkin spelling seen in sheriff-bond context without further evidence. 'Future increase' language means any children born to Sally after Feb. 25, 1799 were born free.
